overview: Sims Limited, founded in Australia in 1917, is a global leader in metal recycling (ferrous and non-ferrous scrap) and the provision of repurposing solutions for retired technology and cloud/data-centre infrastructure. The Group operates wholly-owned metal recycling facilities across North America, Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea (Sims Metal segment), holds a 50% joint-venture stake in SA Recycling (SAR), one of the largest US metal recyclers, and runs Sims Lifecycle Services (SLS), a global IT asset disposition and data-centre decommissioning business. Sims employs approximately 3,900-3,916 people across 150+ facilities in 13 countries and trades on the ASX (SGM) and US OTC (SMSMY, ADR).

business_model.summary: Sims buys ferrous and non-ferrous scrap metal (end-of-life vehicles, appliances, industrial and demolition scrap) from a fragmented supplier base, processes it via shredding/downstream separation technology, and sells recycled metal to steel mills (via electric arc furnaces), foundries and smelters domestically and via export, earning a 'trading margin' between buy and sell prices. Increasingly it also collects and repurposes retired IT hardware and data-centre equipment (memory modules/DIMMs, and prospectively GPUs) for resale, capturing a structurally different, higher-margin fee/resale business through SLS. Revenue is transactional/commodity-linked in Metal (volume x price, exposed to ferrous/non-ferrous commodity cycles) and increasingly service/resale-fee based and structurally growing in SLS, driven by hyperscaler data-centre refresh cycles.

revenue_streams.name: SA Recycling (50% JV, equity accounted, not consolidated in revenue)

business_model.customer_type: B2B - steel mills, foundries, smelters, and secondary metal traders/exporters for Metal; enterprise/hyperscaler data-centre operators and OEMs for SLS
business_model.geographic_mix: United States 33.2%, Turkey 12.7%, China 10.3%, India 6.0%, Australia 6.0%, Thailand 5.4%, Other 26.3% (FY25 sales revenue to external customers by destination)

main_competitors: SA Recycling (JV partner but also independent operator in overlapping US markets)
Numerous regional/independent scrap yards (highly fragmented industry)
competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest listed metal recyclers globally by volume (~6.1m proprietary intake tonnes FY25, plus SAR JV contributing ~5.4m tonnes), with leading scale in North America (NAM plus 50% of SA Recycling) and Australia/New Zealand. In electronics/IT asset disposition, SLS is a top-tier global player positioned to benefit from AI/hyperscaler data-centre growth, particularly in DDR4 memory resale.

moat_factors.description: 275+ metal facilities, 20 shredders and a footprint across 44 countries provide sourcing/logistics advantages (rail, barge, port access) that are costly for smaller independents to replicate.
50% economic interest in one of the largest US recyclers extends scale, market access and bolt-on M&A capacity (8 acquisitions completed in FY25, 5 more in H1 FY26) without full consolidation risk.

100+ year operating history, AAA MSCI ESG rating and #2 Corporate Knights Global 100 ranking make Sims a preferred, transparent counterparty for corporate suppliers with sustainability reporting obligations and for hyperscaler customers requiring secure data destruction/compliance.

Secure data destruction and chain-of-custody credentials create switching costs for enterprise/hyperscaler IT-asset-disposition customers; GPU repurposing certification complexity (an 'order of magnitude higher' than memory modules per management) could become a durable technical barrier if Sims establishes first-mover capability.
Large shredding capacity and downstream separation technology improve recovery rates and trading margins versus smaller operators lacking capital for automation.

weaknesses: Fundamentally a commodity trading-margin business with limited pricing power over scrap metal - margins are squeezed by Chinese steel export oversupply and cyclical ferrous demand
Highly fragmented supplier base with low switching costs on the buy side, keeping intake competition intense
ANZ Metal segment structurally disadvantaged versus low-cost Asian steel exporters, especially amid record Chinese export volumes

SLS/DDR4 resale profits are exposed to volatile and potentially transient component pricing spikes (DDR4 reference prices up >1000% year-on-year per FY26 results) rather than a proven recurring revenue base
No consolidated control over SA Recycling (only 50% JV, equity-accounted) limits capital allocation flexibility over roughly half the North American metals earnings base

growth_drivers: Sims Lifecycle Services (SLS) expansion - AI/hyperscaler data-centre buildout is driving explosive growth in retired IT hardware volumes and high resale values for repurposed DDR4 memory modules (repurposed units up 44% in FY25, SLS underlying EBIT up 84% in FY25 and 247.5% in H1 FY26)

Emerging GPU repurposing opportunity - management is investing in R&D and has begun receiving customer samples to certify GPU recovery/resale as a longer-term (12-24 month) growth vector beyond memory
Structural growth in electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking capacity in the US and announced/proposed EAF developments in Australia/New Zealand, increasing long-term scrap demand
US tariff protection supporting domestic ferrous/non-ferrous premiums and margins for NAM and SA Recycling
Non-ferrous market strength (copper, aluminium) driven by AI data-centre buildout, electrification and renewable energy infrastructure, partially offsetting ferrous weakness
SA Recycling bolt-on M&A strategy (8 acquisitions in FY25, 5 more completed in H1 FY26) expanding network density and product mix (Zorba/non-ferrous)
Portfolio simplification and capital recycling - divestment of underperforming/non-core assets (UK Metal sale, closure of Sims Resource Renewal) to redeploy capital into higher-return growth capex
Decarbonisation/circular-economy tailwinds increasing structural demand for recycled versus virgin metal inputs

business.risk: Ferrous scrap oversupply / Chinese steel exports
business.description: Record-high Chinese steel production and export activity is exerting sustained downward pressure on ex-US ferrous prices and displacing scrap demand, directly hitting ANZ and NAM/SAR export margins; management flags this as the 'greatest headwind' with pricing pressure expected to persist.

Both Metal segment (ferrous/non-ferrous prices) and increasingly SLS (DDR4/component resale prices) are exposed to sharp price swings that can reverse quickly - DDR4 pricing strength that drove FY26 SLS outperformance is explicitly guided to soften in H1 FY27.

The Unimetals UK transaction (sale of former UK Metal business) resulted in a $60 million expected credit loss on the residual receivable after Unimetals entered administration/compulsory liquidation in late 2025, evidencing execution and counterparty risk in portfolio divestment deals.
Severe East Coast US winter weather has repeatedly disrupted scrap collection and processing (cited in FY25 and prior years).

Data-centre refresh/decommissioning cycles depend on hyperscaler infrastructure rollout timing; management cited 'infrastructure bottlenecks' causing short-term unpredictability in H1 FY27 SLS guidance.

financial.description: Reporting currency is AUD, but a significant portion of sales, purchases and net assets are denominated in USD and other currencies; a 10% adverse FX move was estimated to affect after-tax profit by ~A$5.9 million (FY25 sensitivity).

financial.risk: Net debt and leverage through the cycle
financial.description: Net debt of $332.3m at FY25 year-end (down from $411.9m) and total gearing target of <15%; leverage is moderate but earnings volatility in a trading-margin business can pressure covenants/ROIC in down-cycles.
As earnings increasingly shift toward the US (NAM, SAR, SLS), management has flagged the future availability of Australian franking credits on dividends may become constrained.

regulatory.description: Operations subject to environmental licensing/reporting across all jurisdictions (Australia NGER Act, evolving Australian Sustainability Reporting Standards, and equivalent regimes in the US, UK/Europe); non-compliance risk at 150+ operating sites.

US tariffs currently support domestic scrap premiums (a tailwind), but the same policy lever is a double-edged sword - shifts in US or global trade policy could reverse this benefit or trigger retaliatory measures affecting export markets (Turkey, Bangladesh, China).

macro.description: Demand for both ferrous and non-ferrous scrap is closely tied to construction activity, industrial production and GDP growth in the US, Australia and export destination markets; elevated interest rates and softer GDP growth were cited as headwinds in FY25.
Elevated interest rates raise financing costs on working capital/debt and dampen construction/consumer demand that underpins scrap generation and steel/aluminium consumption.

A meaningful and growing share of near-term earnings growth (SLS) is now linked to the durability of the AI/hyperscaler data-centre capex supercycle; a slowdown in AI infrastructure spending or a faster-than-expected DDR5 transition reducing DDR4 resale demand would directly hit SLS profitability.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Long-term secondary/recycled metal demand fundamentals remain structurally positive, driven by growing global EAF steelmaking capacity, decarbonisation policy, onshoring/domestic supply-chain resilience initiatives, and rising non-ferrous (copper, aluminium) demand from electrification, renewables and AI data-centre buildout. Near-term, ferrous markets outside the US remain oversupplied due to record Chinese steel exports, while the IT-asset-repurposing sub-industry (SLS) is experiencing outsized cyclical tailwinds from the AI/data-centre capex boom.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High for the core Metal business - trading margins and volumes move with global steel/construction cycles and commodity prices; SLS introduces a newer, currently strongly positive cycle (AI/data-centre capex and component pricing) that is itself subject to its own boom-bust dynamics (e.g., guided DDR4 volume softening in H1 FY27).
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - indirectly through construction activity, industrial demand and cost of debt; net debt position of ~$300-330m means direct rate sensitivity is manageable but not negligible.
key_input_costs: Scrap metal purchase price (largest single cost/input)

recent_developments.event: Sims reported FY2026 full-year results (year ended 30 June 2026): sales revenue $8,007.5m (+6.9%), underlying EBIT $468.0m (+167.6% vs FY25, beating prior guidance of $420-435m), underlying NPAT $289.1m (+247.9%), statutory NPAT $245.3m (vs $2.4m in FY25), ROIC 11.7% (vs 4.5% FY25, now exceeding cost of capital), full-year dividend $0.34/share fully franked (13th consecutive year of dividends declared).

Stock fell ~12-13% on results day despite the earnings beat, driven by weaker-than-expected H1 FY2027 guidance for Sims Lifecycle Services of $75-90m underlying EBIT, reflecting expected reduced high-speed DDR4 volumes versus the exceptionally strong H2 FY26 comparative and short-term data-centre refresh-cycle timing variability.

Company hosted a Sims Lifecycle Services investor day in Nashville, highlighting GPU repurposing as a longer-term growth opportunity beyond DDR4 memory, noting certification complexity for GPUs is an order of magnitude higher than memory modules; R&D underway with customer samples being evaluated.

H1 FY26 results: underlying NPAT up 70.9% to $60.0m, underlying EBIT up 65.9% to $121.1m; statutory NPAT was a loss of $(29.9)m due to $41.1m unrealised derivative losses and a $60m expected credit loss on the residual Unimetals (UK) receivable; interim dividend raised 40% to 14 cents per share fully franked.

Unimetals Recycling (UK) Ltd, the buyer of Sims' former UK Metal business, entered compulsory liquidation after failing to secure refinancing, triggering the $60m expected credit loss recognised in Sims' H1 FY26 results.

Sims progressively upgraded FY26 underlying EBIT guidance during the year (from an initial $165-185m range) on the back of stronger non-ferrous pricing and exceptional SLS/DDR4 momentum, ultimately delivering well above upgraded guidance.

Completed sale of the UK Metal business (simplifying the portfolio) and closed Sims Resource Renewal (ceased development of plasma-assisted gasification technology for automotive shredder residue), recognising a $21.2m non-cash write-off plus $3.9m closure costs.

SA Recycling (50% JV) completed 8 bolt-on acquisitions in FY25 and a further 5 in H1 FY26, expanding network density and non-ferrous/Zorba product mix; SAR's contribution to Group underlying EBIT rose from $102.2m (FY24) to $120.0m (FY25) and to $59.0m in H1 FY26 alone (vs $47.4m H1 FY25).

Board renewal continued: Grant Dempsey (chair of Audit & Risk Committee) appointed non-executive director of a2 Milk Company from September 2025; multiple director changes in FY25 (Rinn and Omachi appointed; Kato, O'Toole, Gorman retired).

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Full Year Results / SLS Investor Day, 19 September 2026

items.notes: Reflects expected reduction in high-speed DDR4 resale volumes compared to the exceptionally strong H2 FY26 comparative, plus short-term variability in hyperscaler data-centre decommissioning/refresh cycle timing; this guidance drove the ~12-13% share price decline on results day despite the FY26 earnings beat.
Management guided D&A broadly flat year-on-year.
Supported by AI infrastructure buildout, electrification and renewables demand for copper and aluminium; expected to keep delivering strong trading margin contributions across NAM, ANZ and SAR.

Record-high Chinese steel exports remain the primary headwind; medium-term relief anticipated from mill upgrades and new EAF capacity in the region, but near-term pricing pressure expected to persist with limited further downside as prices approach market floors.
Tariffs continue to protect US domestic steel/aluminium industries and support local ferrous scrap demand and the domestic shred sales premium.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Stephen Mikkelsen characterised FY26 as validation of the turnaround strategy, with underlying EBIT up 167.6% to $468.0m and ROIC (11.7%) now exceeding the Group's cost of capital for the first time in several years. Management emphasised that SLS's exceptional FY26 performance (DDR4 pricing up >1000% year-on-year, repurposed units up strongly) was partly cyclical and guided conservatively for H1 FY27 given data-centre refresh-cycle timing variability, while flagging GPU repurposing as a longer-dated (12-24 month) growth opportunity requiring significant certification investment. Management reiterated confidence in long-term structural tailwinds (EAF capacity growth, decarbonisation, onshoring, AI-driven non-ferrous and repurposed-unit demand) while acknowledging Chinese steel export oversupply as the primary near-term headwind for ANZ and export-exposed NAM/SAR volumes.

bull_case: SA Recycling JV and North America Metal delivered a dramatic earnings turnaround (NAM underlying EBIT +735.7% in FY25, SAR contribution +17.4%), demonstrating the benefits of a disciplined, higher-margin unprocessed-scrap sourcing strategy that management can continue to execute

Sims Lifecycle Services provides genuine, structurally differentiated exposure to the AI/hyperscaler data-centre capex boom - DDR4 resale pricing strength and the nascent GPU-repurposing opportunity offer a multi-year growth runway largely uncorrelated with the cyclical metals business

ROIC of 11.7% in FY26 now exceeds cost of capital for the first time in years, and net debt has been reduced through portfolio simplification (UK Metal exit, SRR closure) and strong free cash flow generation, giving balance sheet capacity for further growth capex and shareholder returns

Long-term secular tailwinds - EAF steelmaking capacity growth, decarbonisation policy, onshoring/domestic supply-chain resilience and electrification-driven non-ferrous demand - support structurally rising demand for recycled metal inputs
13-year consecutive dividend track record with FY26 dividend up substantially (23c FY25 to 34c FY26), reflecting management's commitment to capital returns alongside growth investment
bear_case: The stock fell ~13% on FY26 results day despite a large earnings beat, showing the market is pricing SLS/DDR4 strength as unsustainable and sensitive to guidance disappointment - a repeat of soft SLS guidance could weigh heavily on the shares

Core Metal business (especially ANZ) remains structurally pressured by record Chinese steel export oversupply with no clear near-term resolution, and trading margins are inherently thin and commodity-price dependent with limited pricing power

SLS earnings quality is uncertain - the FY26 outperformance was driven by an extraordinary (>1000% YoY) spike in DDR4 component prices that management itself guides to soften, and the GPU repurposing opportunity is unproven, early-stage and faces certification complexity 'an order of magnitude higher' than memory

The Unimetals UK receivable write-off ($60m expected credit loss) illustrates execution/counterparty risk in Sims' portfolio-simplification divestment strategy, and further legacy asset disposals could carry similar risk

Only 50% economic ownership of SA Recycling (equity-accounted JV) limits Sims' direct control and consolidated capital allocation flexibility over roughly half of its North American metals earnings base, and reliance on a JV partner for a large share of growth capex/M&A decisions
